Clair Obscur feels like one of those games that shouldn’t exist, but somehow does because a bunch of passionate weirdos decided “yeah, why not?”

The dev story alone is wild:
A French dude who speedruns Sekiro gets tired of his job at Ubisoft and just… quits to make his dream game. He calls his old university buddy, who ends up becoming the lead tech. He finds a musician on SoundCloud who makes the entire OST. He finds a girl on Reddit who agrees to voice the demo for free and she eventually becomes the lead writer.

Then they hire like thirty fresh grads who are all in over their heads but clearly giving it everything they’ve got. And member number thirty-three? A dog. Literally credited as the Happiness Manager in the end credits.
And the crazy part is: the game actually turned out great. Stylish, unique, full of heart, exactly the kind of thing you get when people make something becau

Every dialogue, every pause, every breath matters. And that soundtrack - melancholic, jazzy, with a touch of saxophone - when was the last time you heard something like that in a video game? I’m sure it’s going to get an award at [b]The Game Awards[/b]. It deserves one. (i'm absolutely sure that game will win GOTY award).

The engine is insane, and so is the combat. It’s a mix of tactical rhythm and action, something close to Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, yet completely its own thing. First of all, Expedition 33 is an excellent game. The visuals, the Belle Époque–inspired art direction, and the music are all impressive. In terms of gameplay, it pushes the JRPG formula further (without the improved parry-counter and dodge system, it would’ve felt like another Persona 5 to me), but overall it’s still very solid.

However, the flaws in the story completely overshadow everything the game does well.

The opening of Expedition 33 is incredibly strong, the worldbuilding is captivating, the emotional setup is powerful, and the presentation is gorgeous. I have spent many hours with this game, yet I still struggle to understand its appeal as a Game of the Year.

The game’s insistence on mandatory parrying and dodging strikes me as fundamentally misguided. At least in an ACT title, players are granted broader freedom of movement, greater tactical flexibility, and far more immediate and satisfying feedback. By comparison, compressing such mechanics into a rigid turn-based framework only highlights their limitations rather than their strengths.

The backgrounds and skyboxes are beautifully vibrant. The whole world is absolutely 10/10 one of the greastest works of art in video gaming.

The music is absolutely gorgeous constantly. It personally isn't my taste, I prefer more traditional video game music over orchestra, but that

It's beautiful visually and the music is great. There are great ideas and implementations spread throughout. I'm a fan of parries and dodges, particularly as a late Sekiro convert. Some of these aspects do also become tiresome as you spend more and more time with them, but not to the point that I would call them a detriment.

Mechanically, my main complaints are:

I hate the parry. Every major boss in the game, post mid-game comes down to this one fact. Can you parry. That's it. NOT character build, NOT party synergy - just parry. I'm sick of it and I haven't finished the game because I am bored and tired of having to learn the attack patterns of every boss in order to beat their long attack chains. I don't want to have to memorize every single boss. It's not fun. 

The graphics are amazing. The story is amazing. I hate the combat mechanics! It has turned this game into a serious, serious disappointment. I really hope in the future they make just pure turn based games. I really hope other games do not follow this mechanic. I will not be buying them if I see it.

If I could leave a mixed review, I would, but ultimately, I believe Expedition 33 is flawed to its core, making me sway more negatively than positively. It's understandable why people like this game; the best part is, without a doubt, its soundtrack. It's phenomenal aside from the song during the Renior fight and the yoinky-sploinky brown chocolate log combat music in the Ancient Sanctuary. The art direction in this game is also great; there are some really amazing-looking areas. Also, the performance is awful. Being an Unreal Engine 5 game, it runs like ♥♥♥♥ without using upscaling. But it's still a JRPG, and we ALL know that for about 98% of them, they're horrendous. So when a game that does something with a singular ounce of creativity or depth comes in, the innovation/content/quality-starved JRPG fans, combined with the cesspool of armchair psychiatrist redditors, flock to this game,

Expected a cool strategy based turnbased-combat RPG, with beautiful visuals, music and story, but got Elden Ring DLC as a turnbased game, zero strategy, because you can beat the whole game by just parrying. You just have to memorize all the terribly telegraphed attack-annimations.
The Visuals, Music and Story are still top of the line, no question, but the combat system really ruins it.

I probably would have been less harsh on this game if it was not so overhyped. The problem is that so many people praised it like it was a masterpiece and one of the deepest story experiences in gaming, so naturally my expectations were much higher.

What I got instead was a game with good gameplay and a very strong soundtrack, but a story that felt vague, forced, and emotionally artificial. The music constantly tries to make scenes feel deep and melancholic, but for me the story and characters did not earn those emotions. A lot of the dialogue felt more focused on sounding mysterious and poetic than actually building depth.

I do not think this is a bad game. It is above average, and I can understand why some people love it. But because of how heavily it is praised, the disappointment hit harder for me. In the end, I cannot recommend it.

6/10 – 6.5/10

Combat just wasn't fun for me. Nothing really matters except your ability to parry/jump on the defense (QTE). If you fail at the quick time events, one of your characters can be one-shotted by some boss. If you only succeed, then you won't receive damage at all and what you do during the offense (tactics) doesn't matter. Mixing in QTEs in the turn based combat is a cool idea, but I believe it should have only had an effect on the offense, so that strategy is more important than timing skills.

I'm in the minority here, I know, but I don't think this game was very "good". It’s frustrating and doesn’t respect your time or intelligence. It’s got great ideas, with mostly good execution, but can’t deliver on its many promises in a lot of key areas. Should you play this? Probably. Everybody else is doing it.

But I can’t recommend it. It’s a beautiful EXPERIENCE, but only a half-decent GAME.
